pending_items.title: Why solidarity with Gaza failed to stop the genocide
pending_items.content:
On 12 November, Israel attacked Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, killing six Palestinians and injuring dozens more.

Among those killed were Saif Abu Hatab, who was awaiting surgery, and Dr Rizq Abu Shaeira, a surgeon working at the hospital. Other surgeons, patients and their companions were among the injured.

Beyond the reporting and familiar condemnations from human rights organisations and UN agencies, the attack appeared to provoke little reaction, let alone meaningful political consequences for Israel.

After Israel systematically attacked and dismantled Gaza's healthcare system from 2023 through 2025, why would another attack on another hospital warrant a different response?

Still, this is precisely the moment to ask some serious questions about the international political order and its response to Israel's genocide in Gaza .

How have we reached a point where an attack on a hospital, killing patients and the doctors treating them, can pass almost unnoticed?

Three years into the genocide, the growing numbness and indifference towards Gaza are increasingly difficult to ignore. Since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, more than 1,600 Palestinians have reportedly been killed and 5,833 injured, while the humanitarian situation remains catastrophic.

Much of Gaza lies in ruins, its healthcare system devastated, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians remain displaced. With winter arriving, heavy rains have flooded displacement camps, leaving families who have already lost their homes struggling to find somewhere dry and safe to sleep.

None of this was unexpected, yet Israel's continuous restrictions on essential supplies and the destruction of infrastructure have left people exposed to conditions that could have been prevented.

What is particularly disturbing is that Palestinians are now enduring these conditions with even less international attention than before.

The ceasefire has helped create the impression that the worst is over, allowing governments and political leaders to speak of rehabilitation and peace despite the continued destruction of Palestinian life.

Against the backdrop of the Israeli elections , political attention has increasingly shifted towards Israel's domestic politics, electoral alliances and the possibility of replacing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

For many, the prospect of removing the government responsible for so much destruction offers a sense of hope and political urgency. And while a change of government could bring some relief, there is a danger in treating it as a turning point for Palestinians.

The siege of Gaza did not begin with Netanyahu, Ben Gvir or Smotrich, nor did the occupation and dispossession of Palestinians.

These policies have been pursued and maintained by successive Israeli governments, including those presented as more moderate. Yet, as the debate increasingly centres on who will govern Israel next, the question of what will change for the Palestinians, and particularly for those in Gaza, risks being pushed aside.

The growing indifference towards Gaza cannot be understood simply as a consequence of declining media attention or public exhaustion.

During the first year of the genocide, millions of people took to the streets, students established encampments , workers organised, and campaigns demanding an end to military and institutional ties with Israel gained momentum.

Gaza was at the centre of global attention, and the evidence of Israel's atrocities was impossible to ignore. Yet, none of this brought the genocide to an end.

This is a reality we need to confront. The problem cannot simply be that people are no longer paying attention.

For a considerable period, they were paying attention, protesting and demanding action. And still, Israel continued its attacks and destruction, with the political and military support of some of the world's most powerful governments.

Gaza was at the centre of global attention, and the evidence of Israel's atrocities was impossible to ignore. Yet, none of this brought the genocide to an end

This is not to dismiss the significance of these mobilisations. Steps have indeed been taken within universities, trade unions and other institutions to challenge their complicity and cut ties with Israel .

Some campaigns have secured concrete changes, while others continue to organise towards goals that may take years to achieve.

Political struggles do not produce all their outcomes overnight, nor should their significance be measured solely by immediate results.

But acknowledging these achievements should not prevent us from recognising the enormous gap between the scale of global mobilisation and the reality facing Palestinians in Gaza.

Three years into the genocide, despite extensive documentation of atrocities, mass public opposition to the genocide and international legal proceedings, Israel has not faced consequences sufficient to stop the violence, and meanwhile, trucks carrying tents, blankets, mattresses and other essential supplies remain stranded outside Gaza, as Israeli restrictions continue to obstruct their entry.

This should trouble us profoundly, not because the mobilisations have been meaningless, but because of what their inability to stop the genocide reveals about the broader political and economic order that has enabled it to continue.

The problem is not that the world has failed to understand what is happening in Gaza. It is that this knowledge has not translated into the political will to stop it.

What is particularly alarming is how quickly Gaza fades from public attention when Palestinians are no longer being killed in large numbers, even as the conditions that have made such violence possible remain unchanged.

Mass killing cannot be the only catalyst for outrage and mobilisation, nor can our attention to Gaza depend on the scale of Palestinian suffering at any given moment.

This brings us to another difficult question: what does solidarity with Gaza look like after three years of genocide, political exhaustion and mobilisation that, despite its scale, has failed to bring an end to the violence?

And how can it be sustained when Palestinians are no longer being killed in the hundreds in a single day, but continue to die from frequent Israeli air strikes, the collapse of healthcare and the destruction of the basic conditions necessary for life?

Palestinians should not have to experience another massacre to bring people back into the streets. Nor should solidarity depend on a constant supply of images and testimonies of death and destruction.

While some of us have the privilege of turning away, Palestinians in Gaza must continue living through what the rest of the world can choose to stop watching

The past three years have demonstrated the limitations of a politics that relies on shock and bursts of outrage to sustain itself.

This is not an argument against demonstrations, but an invitation to think more seriously about how solidarity can become an ongoing political commitment rather than a reaction to particular moments of violence.

How do we organise for changes that may take years, while refusing to accept that Palestinians should have to wait years for their lives to be protected? How do we sustain political pressure while confronting the limitations of the strategies pursued so far?

These questions have no easy answers. But they are precisely the questions we need to confront, rather than waiting for another massacre to return Gaza to the centre of public attention. Solidarity cannot be reduced to witnessing Palestinian suffering.

It must also engage with Palestinian political demands and challenge the conditions that have made this destruction possible.

The attack on Nasser Hospital should have been intolerable. So should the continued killing of Palestinians after the ceasefire and the flooding of displacement camps.

Exhaustion is understandable, particularly after three years of witnessing such immense suffering. But exhaustion is not experienced equally.

While some of us have the privilege of turning away, Palestinians in Gaza must continue living through what the rest of the world can choose to stop watching.

Perhaps solidarity also means recognising this unequal burden, and asking how those of us with greater safety and freedom can take on more of the responsibility for sustaining political attention and action, even when the urgency of the moment has faded.

Three years into the genocide, perhaps the question is no longer simply how to bring Gaza back to the world's attention, but how to sustain a politics of solidarity that does not depend on that attention in the first place.

pending_items.title: Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
pending_items.content:
Yemen , where civil war broke out in 2014, has recently been rocked by the worst fighting in years. A truce agreed in 2022 between the Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis, who control the north, and forces loyal to the government in the south disintegrated when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July.

In August and September, the Houthis mounted a quick offensive, recapturing much of the western coast, including the port of Mocha, putting it within close range of ships passing the strategically important Bab el-Mandab strait.

The Houthis are now targeting Aden, Yemen’s colosecond city and seat of its internationally recognised government since the group took the capital Sanaa 12 years ago.

Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their decade-long siege of Taiz, blocking the road to Aden and raising the prospect of its capture.

The Saudi-backed pro-government military coalition contains a variety of armed units and local militias, each with different goals, rival leaders and origins, leading to infighting and disorganisation.

Allegiances frequently shift and evolve: the Giants Brigade and the National Resistance Forces were each previously backed by the UAE . The leaders of both, like much of the coalition, are now bankrolled by Riyadh amid its fallout with Abu Dhabi.

With fighting spread across multiple front lines, here’s an overview of the most important military and political parties involved in the conflict.

Yemen has been officially administered by the eight-member Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) since 2022, chaired by politician Rashad al-Alimi. It is recognised internationally as the government of Yemen, and backed by Saudi Arabia.

Several PLC members lead their own military units, which nominally make up Yemen’s armed forces but are ultimately accountable to their commanders and their external backers.

The Giants Brigades (Al-Amaliqa), mostly drawn from southern Salafi and tribal fighters, are estimated to number 20,000–30,000 fighters. Their leader is Abdulrahman al-Muharrami, better known as Abu Zaraa, a Salafi cleric turned military commander from Lahij governorate who sits on the PLC.

The units were originally armed, trained and funded by the UAE and were long affiliated with the STC, but have been on the Riyadh payroll since Abu Dhabi pulled back from Yemen earlier this year.

Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King's College London's School of Security Studies, told Middle East Eye that "Riyadh has been able to co-opt individuals such as Abu Zaraa, but it has not been able to absorb their entire networks. The Giants retain their southern identity and longstanding Emirati relationships."

The force is among the coalition's best-equipped: it was key to the recapture of the western coast from the Houthis in 2017 (albeit with aerial support from the UAE), and is integral to the current government's defence of Aden.

Many of the Giants’ fighters identify as southerners and are reluctant to defend territory beyond southern Yemen.

Islah (formally known as the Yemeni Congregation for Reform) is a Sunni political movement with historic ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. It also includes Salafi and tribal fighters.

Despite its ideological affiliations, it is crucial to Riyadh's political and military network in Yemen. The UAE, however, has long opposed Islah, and has lobbied abroad for it to be classified as a terrorist group.

Islah is especially influential in Taiz, where it dominates the government's security operation, including the Taiz Military Axis, which coordinates the military units defending the city against 11 years of Houthi siege.

Homeland Shield (Quwat Dira al-Watan, also known in English as the National Shield Forces) is led by commander Abdulrahman al-Lahji.

It was established in 2022 and formalised as a military unit the following year with the backing of PLC chair Rashad al-Alimi. Its estimated 30-40,000 fighters principally come from Salafi and tribal communities in the eastern Hadramaut and al-Mahrah governorates.

Homeland Shield was key to the recapture of Hadramaut from the STC-affiliated forces in January and is now fighting the Houthis along the eastern frontline. It has also been used as a police force to quell internal discontent, including in crackdowns on rallies of STC supporters.

The National Resistance Forces are led by Tareq Saleh, nephew and former aide of President Ali Abdullah Saleh, who was driven from power in 2012 and killed by the Houthis, his onetime allies, in 2018.

Many of its fighters come from the remnants of the former president's Republican Guard, who were backed by the UAE until the STC’s failed putsch in January. It has subsequently shifted allegiances - and its payroll - to Riyadh. Unlike the UAE-backed STC, it nominally supports a unified Yemen.

From its HQ in Mocha, the NRF’s estimated 50,000 fighters controlled much of the Red Sea coastline until their position collapsed dramatically amid the Houthis’ August-September offensive. Saleh fled to Riyadh on 12 September, and some NRF troops have since been redeployed to remote regions of Hadramaut.

Krieg said that the loss of Mocha meant that the NRF had lost "its principal territorial, logistical and political base," leaving the force "severely degraded. The forces retain experienced personnel, but I would no longer regard the NRF as a credible independent offensive force in the short term."

The Hadramaut Tribal Alliance (HTA) is a coalition that wants greater autonomy for the governorate, home to much of Yemen’s modest oil reserves and where there has long been resentment against Aden’s political and military control.

Founded in 2015, its leader is tribal sheikh Amr bin Habrish, who has called for greater local control over natural resources, security forces and politics. Its armed wing, the Hadramaut Protection Forces, sits outside government control but has been courted by Riyadh to counter UAE-backed southern fighters.

In December 2025, the HTA tried to take Hadramaut’s oil fields, sparking the STC’s failed putsch later that month. Bin Habrish travelled to Saudi Arabia in January amid clashes between his forces and the UAE-backed STC. In July, Saudi authorities prevented him from returning to Yemen without explanation.

The rebel alliance is dominated by the Houthis or Ansar Allah ("helpers of God"), which emerged from the Saada governorate in northern Yemen during the 1990s.

It currently has an estimated 350,000 fighters, wants international recognition as the government of Yemen, and an end to the ongoing Saudi blockade, which has caused devastating hunger . The group is rooted in Zaydism, a minority branch of Shia Islam that is concentrated in the northern highlands.

Amid demands for northern autonomy, the Houthis repeatedly fought the Saleh government between 2004 and 2010.

The group, now led by Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, brother of founder Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, seized Sanaa in September 2014. Six months later, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition to restore the government.

In 2022, a UN-brokered informal ceasefire left the Houthis with 30 percent of Yemen, containing 80 percent of the population.

The group has received extensive military and tactical support from Iran , including shipments that allow them to build some of Tehran’s most sophisticated missile and drone systems . It has also received support from Hezbollah . Although the Houthis claim to be Yemen's government, they are only recognised as such by Iran.

The group, whose slogan is “God is the greatest, death to America, death to Israel , curse the Jews, victory to Islam", has attacked Israel since October 2023, as well as vessels linked to Israel and Saudi Arabia that navigate the Bab el-Mandab strait. The Houthis have also repeatedly hit Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s airport .

Throughout its decade running northern Yemen, the Houthis have forged alliances with local tribal leaders, but have also faced discontent from local sheikhs and tribal groups that have been strong-armed by the Houthi leadership in Sanaa.

The Southern Transitional Council (STC) is no longer the force it was 12 months ago but its influence is still felt. It was a political body that emerged in April 2017 amid longstanding calls for a separate southern Yemeni state, which existed between 1967 and 1990.

During the war, it had the political and financial backing of the UAE, which helped it seize Aden in 2019 and become the dominant power across much of the south. It was allied with the government against the Houthis: three STC leaders, including founder Aidarous al-Zubaidi, held seats on the PLC.

In December 2025, its Hadrami Elite Forces seized territory in Hadramaut and al-Mahra governorates, which would have given it control over almost all of the former state of South Yemen.

This sparked fury from Riyadh, which launched air strikes against the STC and backed a counteroffensive led by the Homeland Shield and others. STC forces retreated and were then forced to disband. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi, was forced to leave the PLC and charged with treason. The UAE pulled all resources from Yemen, cutting military funding as well as its provision of public services, including hospitals.

The STC now lacks its previous military and political power. Many of its affiliated fighters are now allied with the pro-government bloc and paid by Saudi Arabia.

But support for the goal of an independent South Yemen remains strong in Aden and surrounding areas, where there have been pro-STC protests , prompting violent crackdowns from pro-government security forces. The group has also reopened branches across the country.

"The Saudis succeeded in dismantling much of the STC’s institutional architecture in January, but they have not dismantled the social, political and military networks on which it was built," Krieg says.

"The southern question remains unresolved, and Saudi Arabia’s inability to deliver security, economic stability and effective governance has arguably reinvigorated southern separatism."

Al-Qaeda in the Arab Peninsula (AQAP) still has a presence in parts of southern Yemen, despite years of counterterror operations. It wants to establish an Islamic emirate throughout the Arabian Peninsula, and is known for its mass casualty attacks on civilians.

But the group is far weaker than it was a decade ago, when it seized and ruled the port of Mukalla for a year, as well as parts of southern and eastern Yemen. Today it has bases in mountainous outposts, from which it conducts a low-level insurgency, targeting southern government-aligned forces.

AQAP hasn't had direct clashes with the Houthis since 2022, with whom it has conducted prisoner exchanges and has been accused of coordinating smuggling operations.

pending_items.title: Iqbal in space: Urdu poet’s verses unite India, Pakistan beyond Earth
pending_items.content:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Floating inside China’s Tiangong space station on Wednesday, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali turned to a poet from home.

Wearing a blue flight suit bearing the green-and-white Pakistani flag and surrounded by five Chinese crewmates, Pakistan’s first astronaut recited a couplet by Muhammad Iqbal, the country’s national poet.

“Sitaron se aage jahan aur bhi hain / abhi ishq ke imtihan aur bhi hain,” Ali said.

He paused briefly between the two lines before repeating the opening phrase and completing the verse, trying to steady himself as he floated.

He then smoothly switched to Mandarin, translating the couplet’s meaning to his Chinese crewmates.

“Countless worlds lie beyond the stars, and countless trials are still ahead,” he said.

As he finished with a thank-you and a smile, the crew broke into applause and cheers before coming together for midair hugs and laughter.

But this was not the first time Iqbal’s poetry had travelled from Earth into orbit.

The first such exchange took place in 1984, when Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian in space, invoked the poet’s words while responding to then Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi’s question about how India looked from above.

In 1997, another Indian-born astronaut, Kalpana Chawla, heard Iqbal’s poetry quoted by then-Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral during a conversation from orbit. Gujral recited the opening line of the same couplet Ali would read to his Chinese crewmates decades later.

Iqbal was a poet, philosopher and political thinker whose ideas helped shape Muslim politics in South Asia in the early 20th century.

Born on November 9, 1877, in Sialkot in what was then British India, he studied in Lahore, England, and Germany; qualified in law; and earned a doctorate in philosophy.

Across South Asia, he is still widely known as Allama, meaning the learned one.

He wrote primarily in Persian and Urdu. His Persian poetry earned him a lasting following in Iran, as well, where he is known as Iqbal-e-Lahori, or Iqbal of Lahore.

In 1930, while presiding over the annual session of the All-India Muslim League in Allahabad, he proposed that Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Balochistan be brought together in a single self-governing state, within or outside the British Empire.

Although he did not use the word “Pakistan” in his address, his proposal came to be regarded as the intellectual idea that eventually led to the country’s creation. In Pakistan, he is often described as the man who dreamed of the country.

Iqbal died in Lahore on April 21, 1938, nine years before Partition led to the creation of Pakistan in 1947.

Rakesh Sharma, a squadron leader in the Indian Air Force, flew on board the Soviet Soyuz T-11 mission on April 3, 1984. He spent nearly eight days on board the Salyut 7 space station.

That month, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi spoke to him during a televised conversation.

“Upar se Bharat kaisa dikhta hai aapko?” she asked. (How does India look to you from up there?)

“Ji, main baghair kisi jhijhak ke keh sakta hoon ke sare jahan se achha,” Sharma replied. (I can say without any hesitation, better than the whole world.)

His response referred to Iqbal’s famous poem, Tarana-e-Hindi, written in 1904, which includes the line “Sare jahan se achha, Hindustan hamara” (Better than the whole world, our India).

Later rendered as a song, Sare jahan se achcha was one of the anthems of India’s independence struggle. It remains one of India’s most popular patriotic songs, and the Indian Army band frequently performs it on major occasions.

Chawla, born in the Indian state of Haryana, made her first spaceflight on board the US space shuttle Columbia, which launched on November 19, 1997.

During her next space visit in 2003, she died along with her crewmates when the shuttle broke apart during its return to Earth.

Gujral, who was born in Jhelum, in what is now Pakistan, was fluent in Urdu and had a fondness for poetry. During a conversation with Chawla on board the 1997 shuttle journey, he turned to Iqbal.

“There is a saying by one of our poets who’s very well known in the subcontinent, Iqbal.”

He then recited the opening line of the same couplet that Ali would quote nearly three decades later.

“There are worlds beyond stars. And now you have seen them. How do you feel about them?” he asked.

“It’s a very special feeling … What you are saying does become very literal,” Chawla replied.

“It’s a dome of a dark sky and stars everywhere,” she said. “And it is very much like a storybook.”
